Assessment & Plan (Integrating DDx)

Key findings: Single bee/wasp sting to right arm minutes prior; localized erythema without significant swelling; patient subjectively reports mild dyspnoea and lip/tongue tingling but appears comfortable on video; oral cavity normal; no stridor.  

Working diagnosis: Localized allergic reaction to insect sting.  

Differential diagnoses consistent with transcript and DDx:  
• Early IgE-mediated anaphylaxis/systemic reaction – moderate likelihood given timing and subjective airway symptoms; currently no objective signs.  
• Anxiety/panic attack precipitated by sting – moderate likelihood contributing to sensation of breathlessness.  

Management priorities: Provide oral antihistamine, educate on red-flag symptoms of anaphylaxis, advise urgent ED attendance if breathing difficulty, lip/tongue swelling, or stridor develops; no immediate need for EpiPen or allergy testing unless future reactions occur.  

Management Plan

- Advise OTC antihistamine (e.g., Chlorphenamine 4 mg up to six times daily, or once-daily non-sedating agent) – dose/route/frequency not documented beyond example provided.  
- Educate patient on signs of anaphylaxis (lip/tongue swelling, stridor, progressive dyspnoea); instruct to call emergency services or attend ED if they occur.  
- Provide written/online information link regarding anaphylactic reactions.  
- Monitor sting site; if erythema spreads, becomes hot, or systemic infection signs develop, seek review for possible antibiotic therapy.  
- Reassurance given; encouraged to re-contact clinic with concerns.  
- Follow-up: routine appointment if symptoms persist or recur (not specifically scheduled).

- Mental health support if indicated (e.g., psychologist, AMS support):  Not recorded (patient currently coping; no request made).  
- CTG registration:  Not recorded.  
- Preventive health follow-up booked (e.g., flu vaccine, Pap test):  Not recorded.  

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx)

1. Localized allergic reaction to insect sting – High likelihood; isolated erythema at sting site, no systemic compromise.  
2. Early IgE-mediated anaphylaxis – Moderate likelihood; rapid onset after sting with subjective airway symptoms, but no objective findings at review.  
3. Anxiety/panic attack – Moderate likelihood; history of anxiety and subjective dyspnoea disproportionate to objective signs.
